title: 3-Read Friday #38: Feedback Conversations, Learning Rates, and Curriculum Trade-Offs
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #38 links a coaching deep-dive, learning-rate research, and a curriculum-vs-pedagogy debate. Pete Foster's granular breakdown of his feedback-conversation process prompts Barton to admit 'how little thought I used to put into' this part of teacher development. Dylan Kane summarises research suggesting students learn new material at surprisingly consistent rates once prior knowledge is accounted for. Clare Stoneman challenges Barton's long-held view that maths curricula are generally fine and pedagogy is what needs fixing, prompting him to plan a follow-up conversation with Ollie Lovell on their podcast.
points: Barton credits Foster's feedback-conversation deep-dive with revealing 'how little thought I used to put into this key component of teacher development.'
He highlights Kane's key finding -- that learning rate is more consistent across students than assumed once prior knowledge is controlled for -- as having concrete classroom implications.
He discloses that Stoneman's post genuinely shifted his thinking on curriculum vs. pedagogy, prompting a planned discussion with Ollie Lovell on his podcast.
quotes: Those of you who are involved in coaching and lesson observations will enjoy this deep dive into Pete's feedback process.
It highlights - yet again - how little thought I used to put into this key component of teacher development.

One fascinating finding is that the rate at which students learn things is actually pretty consistent, and it is the initial prior knowledge they have of the upcoming topic that makes the difference to the final outcome.
My view from watching 100s of maths lessons over the last few years is that most of the time the curriculum in maths is okay, and it is the pedagogy that needs improving.
But this post from Clare has made me reconsider this. I will be discussing this with Ollie Lovell in our next monthly podcast chat!
